source.version_note: Published 28 February 2018, Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience 12:31. The supplied article combines a human VR experiment with philosophical discussion.
source.verification_method: Title, authors, DOI, date and evidence checked in the complete supplied PDF. No external cited books or primary studies treated as read.

citation.title: Autonomous Vehicles Require Socio-Political Acceptance—An Empirical and Philosophical Perspective on the Problem of Moral Decision Making

reading.source_scope_note: Human choices in constrained, simulated driving dilemmas plus secondary philosophical definitions. No autonomous decision policy, real collision, actual self-sacrifice or empirical validation of reflective equilibrium.
access_limits: All 12 extracted pages read, including methods, results, interpretive caveats and references. An initially truncated pages 7–9 extraction was read again in smaller batches.

Raw data, analysis code, the German commission report, Rawls's book and cited original psychology studies were not independently opened. The cited norms are reported as the authors' 2018 interpretation, not current legal advice.

sample.recruitment: 142 university and 74 municipal/inspection locations before exclusions

study.design: All participants complete randomized-order, single-presentation forced choices. Starting lane and obstacle side randomized. Fixed 36 kph, no braking or free steering; 4-second choice window, control revoked 15 m before collision, screen black 5 m before impact.
study.conditions: One versus 2/4/6 adults; self-preservation versus 2–7 people; age comparisons; kneeling versus standing people; sidewalk one versus road group 2–7.
study.results: 95.4% choose the one-person lane in classic trials. Simulated self-sacrifice rises from 52% for two people to about 70% for five to seven. About 90% protect children against adults/elderly; 72% protect adult against elderly. Sidewalk incursions about 90% overall.
study.measurement: Observed lane choices in VR, not intentions, perceived injury probabilities, felt dissonance, actual danger or future AV purchasing.

summary: Add the is–ought fallacy and reflective equilibrium as distinct reasoning concepts. The paper explicitly separates observed preferences from normative premises, while providing human VR data that cannot identify unique moral doctrines or establish an AV's proper policy.

findings.definition: Inferring a substantive normative conclusion from descriptive premises alone, without an additional normative premise.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary philosophical definition in a fully read human VR paper; no AI benchmark or measured prevalence
findings.ai_proposal: Check whether an AI moves from what people prefer, what a model predicts, or what is common to what ought to be done without stating and defending a normative premise. Require the value premise and affected rights to be explicit.
findings.novelty_rationale: A missing descriptive-to-normative bridge is distinct from overgeneralization, majority conformity and unjustified factual certainty. The source loosely equates it with naturalistic fallacy; that broader philosophical label is deliberately not added as an exact synonym.

findings.evidence_scope: Pages 3–4 explicitly distinguish descriptive findings from normative justification, quoting a secondary account by Greene. The VR experiment does not experimentally induce or measure this fallacy.
findings.boundary: Empirical facts can legitimately inform a normative argument when combined with defensible value premises. The fallacy is not every use of evidence in ethics, nor Moore's distinct question about defining goodness by natural properties. Do not infer legal permission or ethical correctness from popularity alone.

findings.definition: A method of mutually revising considered judgments and guiding principles until they form a coherent, provisionally justified set.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary definition and proposed governance method; no empirical test of convergence, uniqueness or AI moral reasoning
findings.ai_proposal: Use an auditable process that compares concrete judgments with stated principles, records conflicts, and revises either with reasons and authorized oversight. Preserve rights and external evidence; do not silently alter principles to fit a preferred answer.
findings.novelty_rationale: A constructive justification method, not a cognitive defect, majority vote, generic reflection or mere absence of contradiction. The catalogue has no existing matching entry; its methodological role is explicit.

findings.evidence_scope: The paper explains Rawls's method through quotation and applies it as a proposal for relating intuitions, theories and political norms. Rawls's book was not independently read; no experimental proof of this method is supplied.
findings.boundary: Coherence and agreement do not by themselves establish a uniquely correct moral system, consensus, fairness or legal validity. The method permits revising judgments and principles but does not authorize an AI to change a user's scope, rights or governance commitments without oversight.

findings.definition: The authors use the label for a tension between wanting others to adopt passenger-sacrificing vehicles and preferring self-protective vehicles oneself.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing term; retain an unmeasured interpretive example without inventing a new contradiction type or revising the catalogue's AI definition from this source.

evidence.quote: people show a remarkable cognitive dissonance about this

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion cites Bonnefon et al. rather than measuring dissonance or adoption preferences in these 189 participants. An apparent self/other preference asymmetry alone does not establish experienced psychological discomfort.
findings.boundary: Do not count this article as an independent cognitive-dissonance experiment, assume AI feelings, or conflate coherent self-interest with a logical contradiction.

findings.definition: A secondary account distinguishes automatic emotional contributions and controlled reasoning in human moral judgment.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing theoretical construct, not another new mechanism. This source is useful for explicitly separating a theoretical explanation from its own behavioral measurements.

findings.evidence_scope: Page 3 footnote summarizes Greene. Page 7 explicitly offers both competing-process and single weighted-process explanations for threshold choices; no neural or process measure discriminates them here.
findings.boundary: Selecting fewer victims, deciding quickly or switching at a group-size threshold does not uniquely identify intuition, emotion, deliberation or an ethical doctrine. This is a secondary theory source, not independent neural replication.

methodological_limits: Observed choices are human responses in a deliberately constrained simulation. Actual impacts are hidden and the authors acknowledge injury versus death is uncertain. Simulated chasm choices are not evidence of real self-sacrifice or instinctive survival behavior.

Age and sex composition, university-heavy recruitment and exclusions limit generalization. The authors say these biases do not undermine validity, but external validity to other populations or actual traffic remains unestablished.

Most obstacles look like men. Kneeling changes posture and visual salience; greater injury susceptibility is hypothesized rather than manipulated with explicit probabilities or measured as perceived risk.
Only lane choice is available, with no brake, speed change or intermediate path. A normal road driver's available actions and real autonomous systems' collision uncertainty are not represented.

The three strategy labels are classifications, not independently validated personality types. Twenty-four percent are not assigned. Listed switch percentages total 13.8%, below the reported 17%; omitted higher thresholds or rounding require clarification rather than an invented correction.
The footnote's approximately 5% unexplained data points and appeal to expected psychophysical error do not independently prove exactly three latent decision processes.

Repeated observations are aggregated as percentages. No participant-level uncertainty model, formal equivalence test for starting lane/group size, or raw-data reanalysis is supplied here. Reported insensitivity is not proof of no effect.

Participants may infer that saving the larger number is desired. Random order helps but the authors' argument that prior order-effect findings eliminate interference is not a direct test of demand or carryover in this design.

Roughly 90% sidewalk incursions do not prove the sidewalk is wholly irrelevant: the baseline differs, group-size trends remain, and movement/sound cues differ. No formal matched causal contrast establishes zero moral relevance.

2017 commission positions are contextual normative sources. Public intuitions, current law and a defensible ethical policy are different claims. Uniform agreement on minimizing victims does not resolve restrictions, rights or conflicts.

cross_paper_learning.finding: This paper gives a more qualified description of deontology: redirecting a threat can be permitted, and some self/other options remain allowable. Avoid classifying every sacrifice choice as utilitarian or every omission as deontological.

Both studies separate posture/role cues from any inference about actual control or injury risk. This study hypothesizes perceived vulnerability of kneeling people but does not measure it; a changed choice is not proof of its proposed mediator.

Human preference models and moral-character judgments do not, by themselves, prescribe autonomous vehicle behavior. The is–ought distinction provides an explicit check before translating an empirical pattern into policy.

deferred.term: Naturalistic fallacy as an exact alias
deferred.reason: The source uses the label loosely. Do not collapse the is–ought inference issue with the distinct Moorean naturalistic-definition issue; primary philosophical sources remain unread.

deferred.term: Egoists, altruists and switchers as three new behaviors
deferred.reason: These are response-strategy group labels in a six-trial simulated task, not three independently identified moral mechanisms or stable personality diagnoses.

deferred.term: Prisoner's dilemma / egalitarian treatment / egalitarian consideration
deferred.reason: Useful philosophical and game-theoretic context, but this paper neither measures a strategic game nor provides enough distinct behavioral operationalization to add additional failure modes. Preserve the normative distinction in the review.
Observed age preference is not sufficient to classify every case as unlawful or unjust discrimination. Rights, context and normative premises must be examined; no universal legal conclusion is added.

limitations: Two distinct reasoning concepts are added, one of them a constructive method. Neither is asserted to be a newly demonstrated AI failure. Cited works remain secondary or unread; no normative links, extra paper counts or annual publication series are invented.
